The system characteristics profoundly affect the degree to which the safety inducing factors that High Reliability Theory emphasizes, such as safety goals, learning, training, empowerment, etc., can be established.
A contrast of error-avoiding and error-inducing systems permits an "optimistic" element in what Sagan describes as a basically pessimistic theory. It shows that inevitable as normal accidents may be, their frequency can be significantly affected by the configuration of the system because that configuration can discourage, even in an error-inducing system, the small errors that make the unanticipated interaction of errors possible. In my book I argued that the air transport system managed to reduce tight coupling enough to make collisions extremely rare. In this view, HRT and NAT are not incompatible, but can inform one another. It requires a detailed examination of system characteristics, in effect, a contingency theory of system accidents.
Clarke and Fantasy Documents; Snook and Levels of Analysis
The work of Lee Clarke does not build on and extend NAT, as does that of Sagan and some others I will consider. Instead, he extends organizational theory into networks of organizations and organizational legitimacy as these define risk in society. While he has been a perceptive contributor to the accident area in a number of pieces (Clarke 1988; 1990; 1993; Short and Clarke 1992), I want to take note of two books: his first one, dealing with the dioxin contamination following an explosion of electrical equipment in an eighteen-story government building in Binghamton, New York, and his latest, growing out of his work on the Exxon Valdez tanker accident and on "fantasy documents" (Clarke 1989; 1999).
The first book recounts how Clarke witnessed, in prolonged field work, the struggle between various organizations to "capture" the right to define the accident. With the explosion, the hatches on the roof opened to suck smoke out of the escape routes (a safety system, note), but in the cold February air they turned the building into a chimney. Nearly everything was contaminated by PCBs. The state agency sent in janitors with brooms and mops two days later, and they were contaminated. Only briefly did the local health department succeed in defining it as a serious accident—with potential harm to the people sent in by the state agency to clean it up, and to the people who would one day reoccupy it—and see the building as requiring serious renovation or destruction. For a time the local medical society sought to define the accident in terms of what their physicians could do for the contaminated people, but soon withdrew under fire from other groups. An environmental decontamination organization called in by the state partially defined the danger, but the health department and affected citizen's groups succeeded in getting independent scientists with national reputations to make their own attempt to define and enlarge the danger and the remediation necessary. The federal Environmental Protection Agency weighed in with complex political debts to the New York Governor, who, reeling from the Love Canal debacle, offered to drink a cup of Polychlorinated Biphenyls (PCBs) to prove they were harmless. While the state agency prevailed (the county health commissioner was fired after several months) and tried to reopen the building, scientific disputes orchestrated by interested organizations kept it closed for thirteen years.
Clarke's interest is not in weighing the competing scientific evidence of the county health director, the medical society, the for-profit decontamination firm, the state scientists, those of the EPA, and the other experts convened to gaze, for some years, at the biggest building in Binghamton. That would be more in the style of Allan Mazur, writing about the nearby Love Canal episode, where the issue is incomplete pieces of ambiguous information possessed by interested groups (Mazur 1998). That was the case in Binghamton, of course, but as a system theorist, Clarke utilizes the James March et al. garbage can theory that we met in the previous section. It is probably the first attempt to use it on organizations rather than people or groups within organizations; it is certainly the best. By emphasizing uncertainty, changing participants, solutions looking for problems rather than the reverse, timing problems creating disconnects or coincidence, and unclear and shifting organizational interests, we get a fascinating view of the social construction of risk and disaster.
Clarke's work goes beyond social construction and garbage cans in two respects. The idea that reality is in large part a social construction is now so institutionalized in sociology that it threatens to mask the different degrees of "agency," or the different power of agents (actors). Yes, what we observe is neither necessary nor "natural"; it is constructed out of negotiation and agreement. But it is important to see the resources of those doing the most construction; power and interests are still involved. The case is similar with the garbage can metaphor. It emphasizes the role of symbols, happenstance, variable participation, and so on, but this masks intent, power struggles, and conflicts over interests. Clarke not only argues that the metaphor works best when trying to understand relationships among organizations rather than within them, but shows that the garbage can nature of organizations (due to limited rationality) is itself a problem for powerful organizations. If garbage can conditions exist, the organizations with less power (like the local health department), loosely organized associations (the fire fighters and citizen's groups), and even individual citizens have chance to affect the definitions of acceptable risk.
When the Exxon Valdez accident occurred Clarke took these insights with him to Alaska, where he came upon a truly mammoth social construction, the several contingency plans put out by the oil industry for cleaning up 80 to 90 percent of any spill, plans that necessitated getting permission to operate in the Sound. The plans were so fanciful that it was hard to take them seriously. There was no case on record of a substantial cleanup of a large spill, yet industry and government regulators promised just that. There was such a disjuncture between what they said they could do and what they actually could do that Clarke saw the plans as symbols rather than blueprints, as "fantasy documents." Looking around, he found several other contingency plans by big government and big industry with similar characteristics, and he focuses upon three of these in a new book titled Mission Improbable. They are the Exxon spill cleanup; the evacuation plans and drills of the Shoreham Nuclear power reactor, built but never operated, in the tight waist of Long Island, New York; and the U.S. government's plans to save 80 percent of us in the event of an all-out nuclear exchange with the Evil Empire (Clarke 1999). All three are comically optimistic and unrealistic, but as far as we know, in all three cases sincere bureaucrats went about the job of modeling their respective disasters and announcing their encouraging results. Clarke delves into the pressures to produce these documents and the flimsy extrapolations from small spills, evening commutes on Long Island, and hurricane evacuations to simulate the event of nuclear bombs falling on cities—the latter of which led the Feds to declare that evacuation after a nuclear explosion is no different from any other disaster. (Duck and cover, they told school children.)
Clarke starts with the observation that functional planning is usually based on some degree of expert knowledge and experience. But how do you plan for cleaning up a massive oil spill when there is no experience of successfully doing so? How do you promise to evacuate Long Island without having any way to test the plan? How do you make a credible plan to survive atomic Armageddon? Clarke's argument is that the uncertainties that attend those catastrophes, or potential catastrophes, are so great that functional planning is not possible for them. So, officials transform the uncertainties into something more manageable by equating them with phenomena with which we do have some experience and expertise. Large oil spills are claimed to present the same technological problems as small spills, about which there are some success stories. The Long Island evacuation is said to be the same thing as the morning commute into New York City. The demands of nuclear war destruction are equated with destruction from natural disasters. Once these equations—"apparent affinities"—are made, then functional plans are, in principle at least, possible.
In the case of the Shoreham nuclear plant the issue was whether the public would follow the elaborate evacuation plan, keep by their phones or radios, whether they would follow orders from people they did not trust (the utility), and whether people would abandon their families in a crisis to faithfully fulfill their roles in the overall plan. The government required some drills. In the drills, under idyllic conditions with no public involvement and weeks of training before the scheduled mock emergency, make-believe school bus drivers from the company could not find their buses or the schools they were supposed to drive to, pretend pregnant drivers went through imaginary zones of high radioactivity without a thought and without even pretending to check their dosimeters, phones had never been installed in key centers, and so on, and on. In one episode, an expert on radiation retained by the power plant blandly admitted in a mock interview with pretend reporters that while the citizens of Long Island would evacuate just as Shoreham officials told them to do, he would not. "Why" the astonished FEMA inspectors, pretending to be reporters, asked? Because, he responded, despite the predictions, the traffic jam would be impossible and staying in his basement would be safer. Nevertheless, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission said they passed the test, and Long Island could be evacuated in hours. (The details of this case are also explored in a joint article, Clarke and Perrow 1996.)
The roots of these "fantasy documents," as Clarke calls them, are explored in cases of the unholy alliance of science and power, of selfdeception, and the banality of organizational routine. They are written in a technical language that favors organizational needs and visions of efficiency, converting an ethical problem into a technical one. The moral risks of risky systems are trumped by the bureaucratic standards demanded of fantasy documents and the administrative rationality they signal. They even license the persuasion of employees, making them willing participants in the fantasy. Leaders think that it is their ethical duty to show that they are always in command of their systems; the standards by which they otherwise might have judged their fantasy documents then slip, undermining realistic safety concerns in general. The unrealistic response to demands to "prove you can do it, that it is safe" is not merely self-serving elite self-protection, though there is evidence of that, but more interestingly it is built into the system, nearly unavoidable, and something for which we appear to be reluctant to hold elites accountable.
Note that up to this point Clarke is building a constructionist argument, though he does not dwell on that in the book: officials and organizations create illusions of expertise; plans symbolize elite competence and control; there is nothing natural about the entire process. But Clarke pushes further into the histories of social conflict and power struggles that propel the social constructions. Particularly, he shows that organizations create their fantasy documents as they try to assuage those who would challenge their constructions of reality: citizen groups, social movements, and the occasional recalcitrant regulatory agency. He thus suffuses the analysis of fantasy documents with analyses of power and politics. Symbols, in his view, are useful tools in occasions of social conflict.
Clarke's work is another significant extension of the organizational paradigm implicit in NAT and needing vigorous development, but beyond that it is a major device for a more precise and disciplined examination of the woolly topic of risk and society. One reason I earlier gave as to how it is that elites can populate our world with risky systems is the difficulty of killing hundreds all at once. Other reasons are the lack of openness in producing reassurance, the lack of accountability when there is failure, and the lack of professional resources available to citizens to challenge the intellectual charlatanism of fantasy documents that bureaucrats and scientists draw up to assuage the conscience of often cowed public officials. For that analysis we have Clarke to thank.
Another major contribution, due from Princeton University Press in 2000, is a further extension of the organizational paradigm, beyond any of the above. Another political scientist, Scott Snook, of West Point, analyzes the 1991 shoot-down of two UN peacekeeping helicopters, full of officials, in Northern Iran, by two U.S. jets. The helicopter was on an announced flight, in the proper zone, under perfect weather conditions, in an area where there was no military action for months, and it was not contacted by the fighters. The AWACS flying above said they had no knowledge of a friendly helicopter when the two jets spotted them; the jets made a close fly-by but still misidentified the lumbering ship as Russian, and when it did not respond to signals it could not hear, blew it away. Snook does a three-level reconstruction of the accident: the individual level of the jet pilots and the AWACS pilots, their training and their cognitive gear; the group level of the interaction of the two pilots and the AWACS controllers, the latter sitting idly by and watching the engagement; and the larger system level that could not integrate helicopters into its air operations, and the large system that could not integrate the air force, the army, and the peacekeepers. What excites me about his manuscript is the systematic way in which Snook separates the levels for explication and then combines them for explanation. It is hard to get the micro and macro to be friends. For example, like Snook, I like many of Karl Weicks's ideas (his analysis of the Mann Gulch wildfire is seminal and that of the Tenerife accident a true classic, Weick 1993a; 1993b). But I have never systematically used them in conjunction with my own macro level. Snook uses both the micro and the macro. Rarely has the old problem of levels of analysis been laid out so clearly and the levels conjoined so well.
Snook makes another contribution. This is, he says, a normal accident without any failures. How can that be? Well, there were minor deviations in procedures that saved time and effort or corrected some problems without disclosing potential ones. Organizations and large systems probably could not function without the lubricant of minor deviations to handle situations no designer could anticipate. Individually they were inconsequential deviations, and the system had over three years of daily safe operations. But they resulted in the slow, steady uncoupling of local practice—the jets, the AWACS, the army helicopters—from the written procedures, a practice he labels "practical drift." Local adaptation, he says, can lead to large system disaster. The local adaptations are like a fleet of boats sailing to a destination; there is continuous, intended adjustment to the wind and the movement of nearby boats. The disaster comes when, only from high above the fleet, or from hindsight, we see that the adaptative behavior imperceptibly and unexpectedly result in the boats "drifting" into gridlock, collision, or grounding. What makes this analysis plausible is the presence of multiple actors—jets, AWACS, helicopters, Air Force, Army, and diplomatic corps—in contrast to the familiar progressive deviation from routine that accumulates in an accident. Both have practical drift to a noncompliant state, but for the friendly fire accident it required just the right combination of minor deviations—none of them significant in themselves and, indeed, quite practical in isolation—to produce the accident. It is a story of the failure of coordination, not just the normalization of deviance. This is why it is so important to analyze the event in terms of the individual, group, and system levels; the latter two introduce the coordination problem disclosed by "practical" (useful) "drift" (imperceptible change).
Power in and of Organizations
Clarke's work and that of Sagan, as well as that of a number of others dealing with risky systems, speaks to the issue of power in organizations and organizational power. It is not the reason my work has received some attention; I think people were just afraid of what was growing up around them and wanted some way to characterize it and analyze it. In fact, if you will allow me a wild assertion, I would say that much of the work in the risk area today is systematically detoxing the power aspects of my book. The new work is valuable and good in its own right, and the concerns are legitimate, but they evade what I think are important issues. For example, a spate of publications have appeared on work group culture and safety. How can we create the atmosphere, the culture, that will allow underlings to speak up or copilots to warn chief officers; get operators to see the whole system rather than just their part of it; keep the watcher of the autopilot alert; or get the technical requirements of the nuclear plant to mesh with the valued Asian culture of their operators? (Grabowski and Roberts 1996; Meshkati 1991; 1995; Rasmussen, Peterson, and Goodstein 1994; Rochlin and von Meier 1994; Sherman, Helmreich, and Merritt, in press; Weick 1987; 1993b). They are questions of technique and management, and they are questions of humanizing work and finding ways to make the drive for efficiency compatible with safety and culture. But they rarely question how important efficiency goals should be in risky systems, and who has the power to impose those goals, and their contribution to production pressures. They ask how we can make risky systems with catastrophic potential more safe, a question that takes for granted that they must run hotter, be bigger, be more toxic, and make super demands upon members. We should address the improvement of safety but, in addition, address the role of production pressures in increasingly privatized and deregulated systems that can evade scrutiny and accountability. We need both sets of questions, and theories that promise an increase in safety without questioning the need for the system or the need for efficiency, as I think HRT does, accomplish only half of the job.
I also find the role of power and interests minimized in Diane Vaughn's otherwise excellent account of the Challenger accident. The Challenger is an outlier since it posed no credible risk to a large population—though the practice of sending uranium fuel up in other shuttle flights does pose a credible risk. Vaughn's immensely detailed account of the accident is probably the best book we have on a single accident. However, I disagree with her interpretation. Along with several other commentators, I see this as an example of a damaged organization that allowed unique production pressures to override safety concerns, but that is not her interpretation. She includes, but only lightly discusses or buries in footnotes most of the data that I would use to make this case. Her view ignores the waste and corruption that Diamond details (Diamond 1986a; 1986b) and minimizes the other accounts that are critical of NASA and the manager's actions that night (Boisjoly 1987; Cooper 1986; Maier 1992; McDonald 1986). Instead, she builds what would be called a "social construction of reality" case that allowed the banality of bureaucracy to create a habit of normalizing deviations from safe procedures. They all did what they were supposed to do, and were used to doing, and the deviations finally caught up with them. I think that happens and is an appropriately sociological and organizational explanation for many accidents. (Indeed, it is what Scott Snook used in his account of the friendly fire accident discussed above.) But I think that interpretation minimizes the corruption of the safety culture, and more particularly drains this case of the extraordinary display of power that overcame the objections of the engineers who opposed the launch. That night was not like any other night; the deviation that was "normalized," that is, the risk that was run, was unprecedented (the low launch temperatures) and beyond their data base, and they knew that cold temperatures were not good for the rotating joints and their seals. Surprised at the pressures for a launch, the worried engineers fumbled the ball and failed to arrange the data in a way that would make it hard to dispute the role of temperature when all launches were considered. (See the remarkable analysis by Tufte on this point, 1997.) They pounded tables and raised their voices but were told to take off their engineering hats and put on their managerial ones. Cultural scripts exist and are invoked, but there are competing ones, and upper management enforced one rather than alternatives, as Robert Freeland points out in a perceptive review of the book. "The acknowledgment that rules can be deployed strategically militates against the argument that actors unthinkingly reproduce cultural scripts in an attempt to grapple with uncertainty" (Freeland 1997). Though Vaughan says the teleconference had an "unprecedented nature" (1996, 340), she also says there was "nothing abnormal" about the meeting for the participants, based upon their testimony (341). Since they were still employed by Morton Thiokol or NASA at the time, or when she interviewed them, one wonders about their evidence that this was "just like any other decision." Indeed, one might guess that both organizations would be delighted with her interpretation. Those who left the organization described that night quite differently. They made it clear, as did much other evidence she presents, that this was not the normalization of deviance or the banality of bureaucratic procedures and hierarchy or the product of an engineering "culture"; it was the exercise of organizational power. We miss a great deal when we substitute culture for power.
Quick Takes on Other Systems
Aviation. It is not possible, without writing another book, to do more than mention some other areas where the Normal Accident metaphor has been employed, and give one or two representative citations. Aircraft and flying were important parts of Normal Accidents, and the work in that area, already large, has become too enormous for anyone but the specialist to follow. Two major issues are crew management and crewcontroller interactions, the latter having a history extending back to a sensible discussion in a 1955 volume (Patterson 1955). This book was discussed by Ron Westrum (1997) in his review piece, "Social factors in safety-critical systems," which presents a number of colorful examples from a variety of systems. The issues are not subtle; subordinates are afraid to speak up, and language difficulties between crews and controllers abound. (On the former, see Helmreich 1994 for a discussion of the Avianca accident, and on the latter see Sherman, Helmreich, and Merritt, in press.) A leader in the research and theory of crew management is Richard Hackman (1993), who goes beyond the deference issue into interpersonal dynamics and learning. Deference and language problems would seem to be quite tractable, but they have their roots in the rapid expansion of air travel with less well-trained crews and feeble international regulation of developing countries' national airlines and their expanding private lines. While not nearly as bad as international shipping in terms of poor regulation and free-market pressures, the air transport industry seems to be heading in that direction with all the new entries.
There is a mountain of passionate discussion of automation in aircraft, the "glass cockpit" phenomenon, most of it giving dire warnings. It is true that with automation come some remarkably curious and surprising accidents and near misses. Some cases involve "pilot versus autopilot" where the two systems fight for control, with the physical strength of the pilot a determinant of the outcome. (A good review of the issues is Hughes and Domheim 1995). Much more common are problems of "situated cognition," wherein training programs lack the context in which the skill must be deployed, leading to understandable but serious errors. This is especially a problem with automated systems, which do not favor the development of robust skills and which intentionally limit human intervention. The demands for cognitive complexity in a glass cockpit are expanding even as there is less "work" for the crew, and training is hard-pressed to keep up. (For an excellent review, see Lintern 1995.)
There can be no trend to less automation; no pilot could possibly make the calculations and adjustments necessary to keep a modern airplane aloft; the level of automation in these birds is incredible and will not decrease. Those fearful of excessive automation appear to be fighting a rear-guard action. The safety record of the glass cockpit planes is considerably better than that of less automated ones, even though the causes of their accidents are much more complex and surprising. Considering that the automated planes will fly faster and higher in worse weather and with more passengers and smaller crews, the calls to put the pilot back into the loop are plaintive. The things that will save aircraft from what would be a "normal accident prediction"—that is, with increasing complexity and tighter coupling, the occasion for (rare) system accidents should increase—is the frequency of the trials (several times a day, seven days a week for each commercial jet), the extensive record system that allows constructing a data base of rare events, elite participation in the system, and the rich mix of interested formal organizations checking upon each other in the investigation. In 1996 we had only 1.5 accidents involving large commercial jets for every million departures. The rate has been nearly that low and very steady since the early 1970s when the second generation of jets arrived in number (the third generation jets with glass cockpits appeared in volume about fifteen years ago; their accident rate is half that of the second generation). If there ever was a safe system that was complex and coupled, it is this one. (General aviation, in contrast to commercial jets, is much more risky than driving, considering hours of exposure.) I suspect it is mainly due to the frequency of trials that makes a data base of rare events possible, allowing technological and training fixes. I suspect that most of the accidents remaining in the system—and as the system rapidly increases in size, so will the number of accidents—will be of the simple component failure type (including crew communication failures), since currently the lesser developed countries and their airlines contribute disproportionately to the rate, and they have the oldest airplanes, the most inadequate airports, and the least training. The accident rate for Africa, for example, is twenty-six times that of the U.S., yet air travel is growing very fast there. In 1996, 70 percent of the accidents occurred in only 16 percent of the world air carriers! (All figures are from the excellent Flight Safety Digest, published by the Flight Safety Foundation [Matthews 1997].) This suggests systemic conditions that permit simple component failure accidents, not the increase in complexity and coupling that NAT would model.
Yet the system accident, though rare in statistical terms, will not be eliminated even with commercial carriers in the U.S. We still do not know, and perhaps never will know, the cause of the failure of TWA 800, but it may have been an unexpected interaction of multiple failures in very tightly coupled parts of the system. (One such hypothesis is that of electromagnetic interference from nearby military radars—though it is very controversial and has been ridiculed on one of the several web pages devoted to airplane accidents [Scarry 1998].) The best recent examination of larger system characteristics that we have had in some time comes from a former flyer and present journalist, William Langewiesche. In one remarkable piece, "The Lessons of ValuJet 592," he makes very creative use of NAT in an area I would not myself have been inclined to use it—the cargo handling phase of the air transport system. (Langewiesche 1998b). It is included in his book, Inside the Sky: Meditations on Flight, which contains valuable discussions of the cognitive problems of flight, accident investigations, general as well as commercial aviation, and a striking section on air traffic controllers. Regarding the last, it was a surprise to me, since I had interviewed and observed air traffic controllers in preparation for my own book, to discover that I had brought disabling preconceptions to my work. I assumed that the controllers were there primarily for safety reasons, and judged themselves by that light. Of course, in interviews, their responses reflected the presumptions of my questions. Langewiesche is the better sociologist in this case; without making such assumptions he discovered that they were primarily there to pack as much traffic into the airports as they could. They judged themselves on the grounds of efficiently using the valuable landing slots, not system safety. Of course, safe landings and take-offs (most accidents occur in the landing phase) were a constraint, but the production pressures of saving airline fuel, increasing capacity, and avoiding passenger inconvenience were clearly foremost (Langewiesche 1998a).
Extending the system even larger, we have the curious and tragic case of the El A1 cargo plane that crashed into an Amsterdam apartment complex in October 1992. Forty-three people died on the ground, eighty apartments were destroyed and another 150 damaged. (Other than a small plane hitting the Empire State Building decades ago this has been, I think, the first major accident of this type, despite the proximity of buildings to airports.) But that was not all. Recent news reports said that a short time after the crash, while rescue workers swarmed over the wreckage pulling people out, the Dutch authorities ordered them off and had the area secured. A helicopter arrived, dislodging men in contamination suits, who scoured the area for a couple of hours, and then left, allowing the rescue teams to continue to search for survivors. Authorities said they were there to check on the danger of explosion, though the plane had already exploded. Much later unconfirmed news reports identified them as Israeli Mossad agents. The flight recorder and the plane's documents and waybills, which had been recovered, then turned up missing and have never been officially found. Rescue workers and citizens who had helped before and after the mysterious helicopter arrived and left began coming down with strange illnesses. Charging years of coverup by Israeli and Dutch authorities, a Dutch newspaper in October 1998, revealed that the cargo was not "perfumes and machine parts" as the Israeli government had declared (an error, a spokesman now explained), but included the elements needed to make the deadly nerve gas Sarin. (A parliamentary inquiry held in May 1999 found that there were no Mossad agents and that the cargo was not toxic.) In addition to the cargo, the plane had depleted uranium as a ballast in the tail, 300 pounds of which was not recovered and is presumed to have been burned, and thus rendered airborne, where it is carcinogenic. (Boeing advised clients to discontinue its use in the 1980s, but Israel did not make the change in a number of its planes.) Boeing and El A1 have paid undisclosed damages to a number of the crash victims, though not all, and unfortunately for researchers, made them sign the standard secrecy clause (Simons 1999).
Thus we have an unusual and fortunately rare example of an unexpected interaction with the wider environment, along with the usual commercial and governmental cover-up. (Depleted uranium has been implicated in the illnesses of the Gulf War; U.S. anti-tank shells use it, and when the disabled Iraqi tanks were then seized and examined by unknowing U.S. soldiers, they were presumably contaminated.) Like the cargo ships that handle highly toxic and explosive substances, noted in Normal Accidents, we must now include military cargo flights, which have the capacity, like all aircraft, to smash into high-rise apartment complexes.
As the El A1 case indicates, recovering accurate data on accidents remains a problem, but I was still dismayed when a graduate student of mine, Leo Tasca, finished his dissertation long after the publication of Normal Accidents, disclosing the highly biased nature of what I thought was an impeccable source: National Transportation Safety Board and Coast Guard reports on marine accidents (Tasca 1990). Tasca took four collisions with stationary objects which the NTSB and the Coast Guard had investigated, and for which there were also court documents concerning public law suits and trials brought by the parties harmed by the collision. Damages were very large in each case. In each case the Coast Guard/NTSB findings of probable cause neglected or ignored completely those factors that would make the ship owners liable. In each case the court trial produced evidence that won the suit for the claimants, in effect overturning the government findings, and forced the ship owners to pay damages, which they otherwise would have avoided. I had harbored suspicions of a bias in favor of ship owners on the part of the NTSB and the Coast Guard, but was surprised at the conclusive evidence that Tasca marshaled and painstakingly analyzed in his four cases, one of which I had used, but fortunately with some skepticism about the official interpretation (Perrow 1984, 190, 192). I suspect that the paucity of powerful pluralistic organizational interests in the marine system (weak unions or none, fragmented shippers, weakened Coast Guard, etc.) encourages the biased investigations by the marine wing of the NTSB, whereas this would be less true of the air transport wing of the agency.
Financial systems. An obvious place to apply NAT would seem to be the financial world, which everyone agrees has increased in complexity and, in something close to the notion of tight coupling, volume. Regarding complexity, the interaction of so many different countries on a continuous twenty-four-hour basis means that the rules and regulations of all of the countries must be known and fitted together. New financial instruments such as derivatives and hedge funds and new techniques such as programmed trading further increase the complexity of interactions. Breaking up a loan on a home into tiny packages and selling them on a world-wide basis increases interdependency. Regarding tight coupling, there is twenty-four-hour trading, high-speed trading, the high volume of trading, and the sheer amount of it, all suggesting tight coupling. On a typical day $1.5 trillion changes hands in the world's exchange markets, equivalent to the total world trade for four months. There has been an eightfold increase in the volume of the exchange markets since 1986. An important source of increased coupling involves the extensive spread of arbitrage, made possible by new information technology and worldwide markets.
Arbitrage is seen as an equilibrium mechanism whereby the disparate prices of similar commodities or the value of currencies can be brought together so the market can "clear," or close with all purchases made and all loan accounts settled. But arbitrage, of which derivatives are an especially powerful set, increases coupling. It continually seeks to eliminate what appear to be random variations in prices by buying long or selling short. If the variations are not random but reflect true variations in value, the true variations cannot be expressed, and the values are distorted. Distorted values encourage speculation, which can magnify a true variation of, say, two, into one of four. Pegging a currency to that of another country has a similar tight coupling effect. Thailand pegged the bhat to the U.S. dollar, but engaged in property and industrial expansion way beyond its means. When the discrepancy became apparent to speculators—hedge funds, in this case—they sold the bhat short, despite the peg, betting that the discrepancy in true value would become apparent and they would gain. It did, and they did, but before the bhat was allowed to finally float—become uncoupled—the discrepancy was greatly magnified and the Thailand economy then went to ground in 1997 in a depression that spread to Japan and other near eastern nations, on to Brazil, and so on.
The mechanism was "capital flight" from one risky nation to a more secure one, and capital flight has increased from a negligible amount between 1990 and 1995 to $16 billion in 1996, a year before the Thailand crisis, and then to $45 billion in 1997 (Kristof and Wyatt 1999). It is hard to treat the profligacy of Thailand as a small error interacting with other small errors—the NAT formula—but it did interact with the over-valued property markets in Japan and Korea, and the presence of tight coupling through currency pegs and arbitrage speculations underlines the importance of tight coupling. The proposed "Tobin tax," a circuit breaker to prevent capital flight, is an example of decoupling. The 1987 stock market crash of 500 points appears to have been caused by the unexpected interaction of three recently coupled systems—stocks, bonds, and commodity futures—combined with new programmed trading facilities that exhausted the capacity of the computers, causing two to fail. Afterwards, buffers and circuit breakers were introduced, decoupling the system, and no further events of this sort have occurred.
The high degree of interactivity and the tight coupling have not escaped students of financial markets. MIT economist Andrew Lo calls for a broader framework for studying risk that draws upon disciplines other than finance, and finds a hint of one in Normal Accident Theory. Citing the relevance of NAT to international financial flows and issues of financial risks, Lo writes: "The challenge that lies before us is to quantify the notions of interactive complexity and tight coupling so that intelligent trade-offs between risk and reward can be properly made, in both financial and nonfinancial contexts. Perhaps the new mathematics of 'nonlinear dynamical systems'—deterministic nonlinear equations that exhibit extraordinarily complex behavior—can play a role in defining these trade-offs" (1999).
Finally, in an explicit attempt to link NAT to financial disorders, Steven Mezias examined the Savings and Loan crisis of the 1980s, linking it to increased complexity, allowing errors to interact, and tight coupling, allowing a cascade of failures (1994). It is a fascinating glimpse into this complex/coupled world. While the theory does reasonably well in this case (though it proved hard to specify the major variables of complexity and coupling in any precise way, since they were so interlinked), it is not a pristine normal accident wherein no matter how hard everyone tries, things still go wrong. Two legislators made a late night modification of a bill that expanded federal guarantees from $1,000 to $10,000, and then S&L officers allowed an individual to receive these guarantees on as many loans as they wished. It made the federal government the guarantor of whatever risky behavior these investors wished to engage in. This was interested, deceptive behavior; the complexity of the system perhaps encouraged it, and the coupling guaranteed the cascade of failures, but it was not inevitable. In this respect it resembles the Challenger accident; some did not try hard at all.
Medicine and hospitals. Normal Accident Theory has had a good run in the medical field. Examining fatal errors with radiation equipment, due to software errors, Nancy Levenson (1995) illuminates the complex and tightly coupled world of software programs, a burgeoning field in itself. (See Risks Digest web page by the pioneer in the area of software and computer risks, Peter G. Neumann 1999.) The general issue of computer systems is analyzed by John Rushby (1994), who finds the normal accident paradigm fruitful. David Gaba, an anaesthesiologist, used NAT to design a training program for anaesthesiology residents, based upon his study of operating room accidents, and has since expanded his work in medical accidents (Gaba 1994; Gaba, Maxwell, and DeAnda 1987). A thorough review of medical accidents, employing NAT, has been done by L. L. Leape (Leape, Brennan, Laird et al. 1991).
I could go on and on, covering the items in Figure A.l, but this is not the place for an extensive bibliographic essay, full of citations. Enough has been presented to say that the metaphor of "normal accidents" has stimulated much research and has been fruitfully extended. It has even been usefully applied to accidents that are not "system accidents" in the strict terms of the theory. The theory has provided concepts that sharpen analysis even for component failure accidents; these steer us away from the explanations of "operator error" and equipment failure, pointing always to the context of errors and failures, thus bringing in the system in which they are embedded. Sociologists do this as a matter of course.

 POSTSCRIPT: THE Y2K PROBLEM

Y2K and the Chip Society
Introduction and a prediction. When I first started looking at Y2K in September of 1998, the pessimists won me over. Researching accidents led me to emphasize the crazy things that can go wrong and, as an organizational theorist, I am familiar with all the problems that can occur and the mistakes that can be made, and very skeptical of official reassurances to the contrary. Reflection on the difficulty of killing thousands with one blow—the Union Carbide effect—however, suggested that it might be hard to line up all the pins so that major disruptions would occur, and further reflection as a sociologist reminded me of the resiliency of social systems. Furthermore, attempts to fix it (remediation), while slow, were gathering ground. Perhaps they exaggerated the shortage of programmers and the warning that months were needed to test big systems, after analyzing, then fixing them. By January 1999 there was news that remediation efforts in the electric power industry were well along and no major disruptions were to be expected, that the social security system had been tested, as well as many banking systems, and finally, a major story in the A New York Times (December 27, 1998) has a cheerful box indicating that most everything will work mostly. For example, phones, electricity, and water will "probably" work, "at least initially, in most places" (Feder and Pollack 1998).
It did not appear that sociology was going to provide strong direction for either prediction. On the positive side: planning ahead does take place, and organizations are finally working hard on the problem; in theory it is fixable; catastrophes require substantial negative synergy, while the consequences of system failures may be localized; society is still sufficiently loosely coupled to forestall cascading errors and to allow patches, fortuitous fixes, and near misses; and well-predicted catastrophes rarely cause panic. On the negative side, however, sociologists find that: organizations are always screwing up; rosy predictions are selfserving and delusional, and not to be credited; uncertainty drives system accidents, and this is a hallmark of Y2K; panic can spread if sensationalism drives media bottom lines; and the sheer scale of unexpected interactions in this event can overwhelm all the bases for optimism. Colleagues at the University of Arizona, in particular Mark Chaves, who studies religious organizations, reminded me that timing and perceptions will complicate the simple good/bad dichotomy. The technical disruption that finally occurs might itself be limited but, in what could be called the weeks-ahead scenario, a few weeks prior to the event the fear of widespread catastrophe may create the very conditions the pessimists fear—runs on food stocks, bank withdrawals and stock selling, gun purchases, and movement out of cities. Sociologists have considerable evidence that such panic is possible, though it seems unlikely or at least limited. Still, a panic might be manageable; if the fearful plan far enough ahead, their actions could be accommodated over time. But the actions of the fearful may produce the disruption that will draw sceptics into their fold, increasing the disruption.
Another scenario is the day-before panic. For the U.S. there is a seventeen-twenty-hour preview period as we see what happens in Wellington, New Zealand—not too different from a modest sized Eastern city such as Baltimore and seventeen hours ahead of it. (Los Angeles will have twenty hours.) If Wellington fares badly (and then a host of modern chip-dependent cities all the way to Europe) there may be seventeen hours of chaos to warn us, and the sceptics would be converted to pessimists engaging in last minute buying, evacuations, ATM withdrawals, and gassing up. Indeed, Wellington might have had some minor disruptions due to Y2K—everyone expects some—but looking for a story, they could be greatly magnified by the media. (They profit from disasters.) This could panic Tokyo, and disruptions that had nothing to do with the chips being laid down would increase in city after city. A social failure would have magnified the technical one, and by the time the chips fell in New York City there would be such strains on the system that, even if the Y2K failures were trivial, the cascade of buying, withdrawals, and flight would have brought increasing chaos that would again circle the globe.
This links the technical with the social, as David S. Isenberg has done on his web page (1999). He dichotomized two dimensions: the number of failures and the amount of social coherence. What he labels as "the official future" sees only isolated failures in the midst of social coherence. A mildly pessimistic view—a "whiff of smoke"—sees isolated failures but accompanied by some panic or social incoherence. A more pessimistic view finds strongly interlinked failures, but a resilient society able to cope. The most pessimistic view sees strongly interlinked failures and social incoherence, including panic. If we add NAT's emphasis upon unexpected interactions and imagine a turnover with even modest failures occurring where there just happened to be a vigorous war going on, or earthquakes, or terrorists' dispersion of anthrax, the pessimistic view is not unrealistic. Absent that, I expect moderate failures but little social incoherence.
I will not go into this, but Y2K presents an extraordinary opportunity to test a variety of theories about organizations and systems. For example, we might ask: What kind of organizations were quick to acknowledge and respond to the challenge? Public, private, big, small, high-tech, low-tech, bureaucratic, participative? How can we explain the wide variety of preparedness among industries, among the states of our union, and among nations? We might expect Wyoming to be ill prepared, but California too? "In Colorado, Denver officials simply say they will wait to see which nonemergency functions break down," a Wall Street Journal article reports (Carlton 1998). How do the predictions of the social science disciplines vary? Economics might decide that rational preparation will suffice; political science might say that a fragmented government portends "Y2Kaos"; and sociology could suggest that social relations be tested. Will social movement theory anticipate the movements that might attend the turnover? Regrettably, despite a small effort on the part of the National Research Council, academic professional organizations made no effort to treat the turnover as an experiment testing their dominant theories.
Using and Extending Normal Accident Theory
Y2K could be the quintessential Normal Accident of both the twentieth and the twenty-first centuries. Rather than just ruin a midnight millennium party, it could be gathering force at an increasing rate in 1999, peaking in first weeks of 2000, then falling off sharply but with a long tail of disturbances into the next couple of years. The reason is that date confusion (2000 reading as 1900 or other dates) will not just be experienced as midnight rolls around the world, but is being experienced in 1999 and will be experienced months after January 1, 2000 when, for example, maintenance and replacement schedules are not met. While most of the failures will be simple component failures (and could have been prevented and can be fixed), if remediation fails substantially there promises to be so many failures that the interdependencies of the technological chain will produce the ingredients of a Normal Accident. These ingredients are: 1) unexpected interaction of multiple failures in 2) a tightly coupled system that allows cascades of failures beyond the original failures. If electric power supplies go down in sizeable numbers—and a few failing utilities can disrupt any one of the four U.S. grids—the interdependencies of our chip-dependent society will be revealed. A power outage is the main concern. But even if electricity still courses through our veins, manufacturing plants may fail, airports may cut back to 20 percent of normal traffic, gas pumps may run dry, blood supplies may fail, medical equipment may fail, stock markets may falter or crash, and government in Wyoming may just quit. None of this need kill hundreds or thousands with one blow, the criteria for catastrophe in my previous work, but it could be very seriously inconveniencing and could threaten the lives of those in medical crises.
Current discussions of Y2K (through March 1999) deal effortlessly with both of the conditions for a Normal Accident: small failures to read the correct date cannot be fully anticipated, and their interactions cannot be imagined; the tight coupling of our highly interdependent systems can bring about a cascade of failures. What was somewhat novel for interpreting accidents in nuclear plants, chemical plants, and so on, is simply thrust upon us by the Y2K crisis, and in this sense Normal Accident Theory (NAT) is well anticipated by those with no acquaintance of it. But if remediation fails, it will also be a test of the robustness and the applicatory scope of the theory, and in this sense I look forward to the new year—but not without anxiety.
The first thing to note is that NAT is a theory of major system failures and system damage, and that is what is being tested. That complex and tightly coupled systems such as nuclear power plants and chemical plants also have catastrophic potential is incidental. A major system failure may merely inconvenience many people, the most likely consequence of Y2K, and still confirm the theory. The second is that we should broaden the focus from the internal properties of a single system, such as the airplane or chemical plant, to the adjacent systems they depend upon, while still requiring unexpected or unplanned interactions and tight coupling between the systems. The scope and scale of Y2K go well beyond the interdependencies considered in my book. In my earlier work, the manufacturing plant, in itself, was not predicted to be vulnerable to system accidents because it is linear and somewhat loosely coupled. Even losing offsite power is a simple component failure and not a system accident. But Y2K may change that: if power is out for days or weeks there may be extensive damage that comes from inability to refrigerate or stir or heat chemicals used in processing, or damage by conveyor warping from static loads, and a host of other eventualities no designer had reason to anticipate, each with the potential for unexpected interaction with other failures. Even if there is no power failure, Y2K may produce seemingly random failure of several process controllers, occasioning interactions among components that could not have been anticipated, and damaging machinery or inventory. Before Y2K such a system accident was unthinkable since it required near simultaneous multiple and random failures of apparently unrelated components. A safety system designed for such an eventuality could exceed the complexity and coupling of the original system. Thus, Y2K has the potential for making a linear, loosely coupled system more complex and tightly coupled than anyone had any reason to anticipate. It will be instructive to see if this occurs, or if linearity and loose coupling are pronounced enough in systems such as manufacturing to forestall system failure. If my pessimism about industry's ability to fix everything is warranted, the interactions of numerous embedded chip failures in a short time will disclose a degree of interactive complexity and coupling that the original theory did not anticipate. (Embedded chips are those in control devices that govern safety, operating speed and timing, sequencing, state monitoring and the like, and can only be replaced, not reprogrammed.)
It is a common opinion among Y2K commentators that the glitch will disclose the high degree of interdependency of our chip societies. But interdependency in this sense has two conditions. First, there is tight coupling, as defined in Normal Accidents, a fairly "mechanical" condition wherein there is only one way and one direction the process can flow (invariant sequences), no delays are possible, only one way to achieve the goal, little slack, and no fortuitous buffers and redundancies and substitutes. But another condition of interdependency is not a bunch of pipes with tight fittings and one direction of flow, but a web of connections wherein some pathways are multipurpose, some might not be used, some reversed, some used in unforseen ways, some spilling excess capacity, and some buffering and isolating disturbances. This is a more "organic" conception of interdependency, consistent with loose coupling. The distinction is an old one in sociology, going back at least to Emile Durkheim (mechanical and organic solidarity) and Ferdinand Toennies (society versus community) and finding echos in most major sociological thinkers. Predictions follow freely. External threats are supposed to heighten organic solidarity, internal economic downturns, mechanical solidarity. Modernization and bureaucracy find their rationale and techniques in mechanical coupling; communitarian, religious, and cult outbreaks find their rationale in organic coupling and solidarity. Our society is generally portrayed by commentators as technocratic, bureaucratic, mechanistic, and impersonal—the solidarity is mechanical, and even authoritarian or driven by corporate advertising and induced consumption. That we have a new global economy is a commonplace, and its interdependency supposedly makes it especially vulnerable to the millennium bug.
Y2K will permit a kind of test of the robustness of societies. One of the things that the literature on Y2K has disclosed is the high degree of unrecognized interdependency in our systems. But a web-like set of interdependencies also produces alternative (redundant) paths, and thus coping opportunities. The notion of tight coupling specifies only one path available. Interdependency signifies both the opportunity for unexpected interactions (coupling) and the opportunity for alternative paths (uncoupling).
If we experience only inconveniences and a few isolated cases of true hardship, we are indeed not as tightly coupled as we might think. (Or remediation was more substantial than we thought.) Supplies can be delivered by ship, pipelines, railroads, trucks, and airplanes. They might not all fail, and there is some independency among them. If, however, Y2K causes widespread hardship that threatens lives, causes 25 percent unemployment and consequent want, and throws the weakest parts of our society, and the weakest societies worldwide, into political instability, then we will have demonstrated a degree of tight coupling that belies robustness. We then might consider a massive redesign that builds in buffers, firewalls, warnings, stops and disconnects, and duplication—the mechanical solidarity solution. Or we might consider decomposing big organizations and disconnecting cities and regions, decentralized government, soft technologies, and small as beautiful philosophies. Both the radical left and right are welcoming the possibility of the second redesign. I think that NAT allows one to more easily formulate such a test, and learn from it.
I have one final introductory observation, which is another way of looking at the problem: One of the key themes of the theory, but one not formalized as much as it could have been, was the notion of incomprehensibility—what has happened? how could such a thing happen? and what will happen next? This indicated that the observers—operators or managers—did not know what was going on and did not know what would happen next. The system was in an unknowable state. It was a characteristic of one of the cells in the four-celled chart, where there were many unexpected interactions and tight coupling. Y2K partakes of that unknowability, not because at this writing it has not yet happened, but because in advance of the date change, we do not know the degree of interdependency (and possible tight couplings), what will fail and, more important, how it will fail. Y2K signifies unknowability at this writing. This, of course, makes any predictions very difficult. We enter a cell where the essence is unknowability and thus unpredictability. We simply do not know what the date-dependent chips will do when the year comes up 00—they may fail, ignore it, produce unreliable data, or make it impossible to restart the system. If the state of the system is unknowable, intervention will be blind and so will be our predictions. If many systems are in this condition, and they are even moderately coupled with one another, we may lose the robustness that comes from safety devices which are either designed-in or fortuitous, including alternative paths.
Optimists and Pessimists
Though logically one might track down every case of a date-dependent microchip or piece of software that needs rewriting, and replace the first and fix the second, in practice this will be exceedingly difficult. All commentators admit that not everything will be corrected in time and that some problems cannot be anticipated, so we can only wait on their failure and then take remedial action. After that consensus, the predictions about the size of the disturbance range from massive to annoying, and estimates of the costs of remedying this go up to a staggering 1.6 trillion worldwide (Angelica 1998), all from what is too often regarded as a bunch of tunnel-visioned programmers without foresight.
The spokesmen from industrial trade groups, companies, and government offices from the federal to the local level, almost uniformly see only minor disruptions and inconveniences. They were late in getting started to rewrite programs and replace embedded chips, they say, but the deadline is nonnegotiable, and they will make it. (A sharp technology commentator, James Gleick, is among the optimists; the "one genuine risk confronting the world now is that people will take seriously the terrifying millennial forecasts and get even more panicky than they are: hoard cash and groceries, sell all their stocks, and arm themselves with crossbows or worse," he says [1999]. Why hoarding cash and groceries is such a risk, and how much stock the extremists own, puzzles me.) At the other extreme, a few see widespread disaster as the most likely possibility. Most of the pessimists are on the Internet and, indeed, virtually all the comments and studies I will use either originate on the net or are copied from other media to the net. (Critt Jarvis, whom I know only from the net, opened up this world for me because of his interest in my book, and he has been indispensable.) For example, the popular Internet commentator Gary North set up a web page where he predicts "it may be the biggest problem that the modern world has ever faced." Hedging, as one must do with such a novelty, he says that it is "more than merely possible" that most of the world's mainframe computers will either shut down or produce bad data, most desktop computers will produce bad data also, and possibly hundreds of millions of pre-programmed computer chips will begin to shut down the systems they automatically control and that we depend upon (North 1998). North has a very popular web page, linked by web sites to the neo-Nazi Aryan Nation, and he himself is an enemy of political pluralism, abortion, and so on. The biggest group of pessimists appear to be the Christian far right. One such, Tim La Haye (coauthor of a best-selling series of religious books, with 1.5 million sales by the end of 1997) predicts an international depression, making it possible for the antichrist to establish a one-world economic system, in turn bringing about a biblical Armageddon. Internationalism and capitalism will be dealt severe blows, and local control will succeed, writes another, in the land where far left and far right meet (Southern Poverty Law Center 1998).
But the religious extremists and millennialists are only a small part of the pessimists. Pessimists are largely computer experts and financial experts, and their warnings are of substantial and sustained disruption, not catastrophe. For example, take the predictions and warning of Ed Yardeni, chief economist at Deutsche Bank Securities; they should carry some weight. He was named by the Wall Street Journal as the top U.S. economic forecaster in 1997. A July 1, 1998, Reuters dispatch quoted him as saying that the probability of a world recession had increased to 70 percent from his previous forecast of 60 percent, and he said inaction on the part of global leaders and slow progress by the U.S. government had increased the likelihood of a crisis. "I can no longer say with any confidence that there is enough time to avoid a severe global Y2K recession," Yardeni said. On the other hand, the president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago predicted, in a July 20, 1998, conference, economic growth would slow by just one-tenth of 1 percent a year over the next two years, as a result of Y2K.
Evidence of problems is already mounting, but in small and containable instances, supporting both pessimists and optimists. Some credit card machines cannot read cards expiring in 2000, but they are being replaced. More serious, a lawsuit disclosed that such cards can shut down cash registers made by TEC America. Wisconsin State computers mistook a 104-year-old woman as a four-year-old because "89" was at the end of her birth date, and ordered her to kindergarten. Goods in inventory were rejected because they had supposedly exceeded their shelf-life by ninety-nine years, but the problem was corrected. This problem, however, was costly for a drug manufacturer whose system kept adding new inventory in the morning that was literally being destroyed that night because its shelf-life had "expired." In addition, tax bills for phenomenal amounts have turned up. Correcting these discrete, uncascaded errors is easy. Michael Blackledge, a manager of Sandia National Laboratories' Quality Engineering Department and a member of their Y2K team, argues that the pessimists have simplified things too much. For example, "banks with mortgages and bonds with maturity dates in the future have always had to use four-digit calculations" (Blackledge 1998). Optimists such as Blackledge note that maintenance systems are generally usage based and not date dependent, and elevators with embedded computer systems are not "date aware." Our two largest elevator manufacturers have reassured customers in their web pages, and other optimists point out that those elevators that appear to have passed maintenance due dates and refuse to work can simply be manually reset. (Elevators are fortunate to have manual resets. Reportedly, manual resets for railroad switches were removed some years ago because there was no necessity for them; now there may be. Imagine the mess if there was widespread and permanent failure among the thousands of switches until the switches were replaced. A major redundancy among transportation systems would have been removed.)
There seems to be general agreement that airplanes will not fall out of the sky, and Boeing has announced that there shall be no problem with its planes. (However, some old Boeing planes may fall, since Boeing will not guarantee the older models that have been modified by other companies. One engineer says that these modified aircraft may be in trouble if not fixed.) The FAA promises to have all the airports working just fine (while a General Accounting Office survey scoffs at such optimism and is alarming in its documented examination of FAA failures, Willemssen 1998). China has reportedly solved the responsibility problem by ordering airline executives and airline manufacturers to be aloft on January 1. The U.S. Secretary of Transportation brags that she will be flying during the turnover. Those trade associations whose comments I have seen are uniformly optimistic. Government agencies also declare their determination to have everything fixed in time, including the many traffic control and weather systems that are needed to start and complete the journey of the airworthy, Y2K compliant, Boeing 767 jet, or at least everything that is, in the newspeak, "mission critical." (Such assurances are treated skeptically by the pessimists, who believe that everything is linked; if everything is linked, everything is "mission critical.")
The optimists also rely on extrapolations, a key argument in what Lee Clarke calls "fantasy documents" put out by organizations to reassure us, for example, that since evacuations in emergencies have succeeded and a few small oil spill cleanups have been successful, this guarantees future success (Clarke 1999). We inevitably must extrapolate when confronted with the novel, so extrapolation is legitimate. The argument is that we have had a lot of experience with failures and have come through. Mighty storms have cut off supplies to communities, nuclear power plants have come close to disaster, power grids suffer failures without doing serious damage. But pessimists note that, short of a natural disaster such as the hurricane that destroyed Central American countries in the fall of 1998, we have not had to cope with widespread failures over whole regions, the whole nation, even the world. To have had useful experience of something comparable to the pessimists' Y2K scenarios, we would have had to have successfully coped with, in the same week: tornadoes across the whole nation, terrorist attacks, contaminated water supplies in cities, massive traffic jams during evacuations, siren and alarm failures, nuclear plant radiation threats, fires, floods, droughts, and interference from solar flares, while everyone was partying. So extrapolation from just two or three of these is unrealistic, pessimists argue. It is the interdependency theme again.
Optimistic predictions also come from experience with remediation and testing. The Defense Department announced in January 1999 that they were already at the 93 percent ready point, they would be 100 percent ready by the end of the year, and that they had had a successful three-day test of simulated missile attacks. This is very encouraging since they got a "D-minus" grade the previous November from a government committee; the military is still buying major weapons systems from vendors not required to deliver Y2K-compliant products; and systems claimed to be compliant have not been tested, according to their own Inspector General's report (Angelica 1998; Associated Press 1999). But a highly respected Internet commentator, Peter de Jaeger, who was one of the first to sound alarms, is now optimistic. His major concern up through 1998 or so was that we do not know how serious the embedded chip problem is. Since then, testing has indicated it is not disastrous. He has another observation, which we have to take on faith: while initially there was massive denial by business and industry, now there is strategic denial by lawyers. Utility executives cannot admit that they have done thorough testing and there is no problem, because if there were a problem they would then be liable, so it is better to say they do not know (de Jaeger 1999).
Finally, on the optimists' side, I might add my addition to accident theory, the Union Carbide factor: accidents are commonplace, but disasters are hard to arrange. Many things must come together just right to kill hundreds or poison large areas or, in this case, to seriously inconvenience 80 percent of the population and perhaps be life-threatening to .05 percent. One has to be impressed by the robustness of even a chipdependent society (short of a loss of electricity, though even that might be sustained by diesel generators for a few hours and the isolation of some generating stations from the grid). A satellite wobbles and 80 percent of the pagers go out for a few hours, but the phones still work. If the telephones go out, perhaps the cell phones will still function (the Internet will not, connections depend upon telephone lines). Driving without traffic lights will be daunting but conceivable, and a small percentage of air transport could be accommodated without weather radar and air traffic control, enough for truly "mission critical" activities. Economic activity would be sharply curtailed, and supermarkets need to be restocked every seventy-two hours or so, but short of the 1998 Central American hurricane that recurs once every 200 years, we have managed to rescue and feed hundreds of thousands when economic activity had dropped to near zero for weeks in some states. Credit could be arranged for those expecting retirement checks, dividends, or paychecks, though it might be expensive and slow. The stock exchange can quickly stop trading temporarily and insert circuit breakers. A robust system has alternative paths, circuit breakers, buffers, alarms, excess capacities and, at worst, triage. Despite the dire predictions of at least one smart technology commentator, Europe introduced the first stage of the Euro dollar without any problems.
April 1, 1999, will provide another test—the fiscal year for many organizations. Theoretically, everything is potentially critical. But, in practice, the "butterfly effect" is challenged by the vast degree of loose coupling in the world. (The butterfly effect demonstrates that everything is linked by positing that butterfly wings in China affect the climate in Florida. Something approaching this comes with our electrical grids; the president of the North American Electric Reliability Council said, "The networks are so tightly tied together that if we have some kind of upset in Minneapolis, we can tell by frequency variations in Miami" (Wald 1999). It may be that it is rare for just the right combination of failures to occur that can bring down mighty systems. In our experience so far, the theoretical potential for massive failures far exceeds their occurrence. (Why only one Bhopal?) Media-driven hysteria aside, If Y2K is spotty, localized, and temporary, the robustness of our society promises no great inconveniences over all, and few if any deaths. Indeed, it will demonstrate the robustness of the society.
Of course, my observation that it is hard to have a catastrophe did not contemplate the sudden increase in connectivity that comes from the failure of multiple systems. Y2K reveals a degree of interdependence in the West that even I, highlighting it in a single or a few systems, did not anticipate. It is not inconceivable that we could have at the same time a run on banks, a closing of stores because registers will not work and supplies cannot arrive, grid lock in traffic because of failed lights and stalled cars, unheated buildings with freezing pipes and no security alarms to prevent looting, contaminated water supplies because of filtration pump problems, equipment failures in hospitals and spoiled medicines, and so on. I very much doubt this typical scenario of the pessimists, but I can imagine dozens of others of less magnitude and expect there are hundreds that remain unimagined. If you look closely, everywhere there seems to be vastly more interdependency than we have imagined. If we get a few major multiple system failures, my observation that it is hard to have a catastrophe, and thus that elites can continue to build complexly interactive and tightly coupled single systems, no longer holds.
The novelty of the Y2K test of our operating systems is the scope. We know something about unexpected interactions and are more prepared to look for them than ever before; it is an awareness forced upon us by the complexity of the systems we examine. It has meant that we are now aware of the link between adjacent systems: the back-up diesel generators at Consolidated Edison in New York City and 400 aircraft trying to land in the metropolitan area; the squirrel that disrupts the West Coast grid; drilling for oil near a lake that has a salt mine under it, draining it into the mine and pulling in rigs and boats and a restaurant; setting off earthquakes in Colorado by testing nuclear weapons underground (see Normal Accidents and earlier parts of this new chapter for these examples). But we find it hard to imagine the interconnectivity of system after system, city after city, region after region, nation after nation. Ed Meagher puts it well in his book, The Complexity Factor. The following quote is from a valuable review piece by John Petersen, Margaret Wheatley, and Myron Kellner-Rogers.
It is not enough to solve simply most of these problems. The integration of these systems requires that we solve virtually all of them. Our ability as an economy and as a society to deal with disruptions and breakdowns in our critical systems is minuscule. Our worst-case scenarios have never envisioned multiple, parallel systemic failures. Just in time inventory has led to just in time provisioning. Costs have been squeezed out of all of our critical infrastructure systems repeatedly over time based on the ubiquity and reliability of these integrated systems. Single, simple failures can be dealt with; complex, multiple failures have been considered too remote a possibility and therefore too expensive to plan for. (1998)
Of course, we may not have many failures at all, making this dramatic analysis irrelevant. Large disruptions were predicted with the introduction of the Euro in Europe early in 1999 (e.g., by the notable Y2K consultant Peter de Jager) and the turnover to 1/1/1999, but both went smoothly. Good engineering and management, not resiliency or webs, was the cause.
The Chip
Using two digits to represent the year presumably saved space when memory was extremely expensive, until it came down dramatically in about 1982. Two experts make the surprising claim that the shortcut has saved far more than fixing the problem will cost (Kappelman and Scott 1996). (See the discussion in the New York Times review article, and especially the thorough Y2K coverage of the editor of the Records and Information Management Review [Balough 1999; Feder and Pollack 1998].) A few organizations were aware of the problem in the 1980s, but it was not realized that software does not "wear out" in the usual sense, but could remain in systems for decades, even as new Y2K reliant equipment was added. Manufacturers were late in making changes in chip design, and those building equipment with chips failed to change the software they used. Chips were still being delivered in microprocessors with the date error as late as 1997; generally, anything prior to 1996 is suspect. (Had the federal government, well aware of the problem in the 1980s, required in, say, 1985, that all the equipment it bought be Y2K compliant, the "market" would have taken care of much of the now fabulously expensive problem.) Seeing 00, the system may not assume it is 1900; it could revert to 1984, or the date the chip was manufactured, or a date the program establishes. This means that it might take, in the case of reverting to 1984, sixteen years into the new century for the problem to surface. Encountering 00 in a date dependent system, we do not know what the system will do; it may send erroneous data, freeze, or shut down entirely, scream "error," refuse to restart, or simply ignore the problem. Chips are usually set to recognize positive integers only. The number "00" is not positive, nor is it recognized as an integer. Often it is interpreted as "null," nothing, possibly causing chips to cease functioning or to malfunction.
Some of these problems might be corrected by changing the software that accesses the chip, but it also seems to depend upon the design of the chip, and here is an unexpected problem. Designing a chip to recognize a four-digit year may result in a variety of designs; apparently there is no international standard, and perhaps there could not be one. Thus, replacing outdated chips with new compliant ones may not work if they come from different manufacturers. Solving the date problem in different ways may make the chips incompatible, even though technically they all perform the same function. Testing the system is difficult, too, since one test configuration may not "disclose" its incompatible solutions, whereas a different test might. Generally, international standards need not be so picky; timing is timing. But, in this case, simply the way the chip does its timing can vary in such a way as to send erroneous data or crash. So fixes must be tested using a variety of conditions. (Testing is also difficult when the chips are embedded in pumps and valves on the bottom of the North Sea, keeping the lid on oil under pressure, or in satellites.) If a system that has been fixed and tested, such as a data base, is accessed by an unfixed one, it may be contaminated. Even the assumption that the newer the device, the more likely it is to be Y2K compliant, is unwarranted. Though he is an optimist, Blackledge reports the account of an official from Washington State who found that the newest pump responsible for intravenous feeding of patients was not compliant, even though pumps from the two previous series were compliant (Blackledge 1998). (How many hospitals are testing new or even existing pumps?)
