This points to the basic difference between 1) software problems—billions of lines of code in forgotten programs in computers that have not been manufactured for ten years—which is bad enough, and 2) the embedded chip problem—billions of chips that are in controllers, rheostats, pumps, valves, regulators, safety systems and so on, which are hard-wired and must be taken out and replaced. (For a good discussion of the embedded chip problem see Mark Frautschi 1998.) The Cassandra Project on the web describes chips as, "the unseen guardians of our lives. They keep nuclear cores stable; the oil, gas, water, and electricity flowing; they keep intensive care units operating; and our military forces armed and mobile. If they fail, our world implodes. And, embedded systems are located everywhere" (1997). There were 3.5 billion programmable microcontrollers shipped in 1995, and 7 billion in 1996. No one knows where they all are, or whether they are compliant. They cannot be reprogrammed, only replaced, and different manufacturers have different compliance standards, making the fix uncertain. Estimates of required inspections of lines of code and of embedded chips are both in the billions, and fixes needed in the order of one to two percent.
System Illustrations
One percent of a few billion is a very large number, and we do not know the distribution of that estimated 1 percent. The robustness of our industrial system comes from backups, alternative tracks, buffers, and so on. But any one component (pump, valve, generator, diagnostic equipment) will lack robustness and loose coupling within itself. This means that a tiny but strategically placed fault, perhaps .001 percent of all chips in the component, may do the trick. This points to the difficulty of the optimists' data: while most of a nuclear power plant is analogue, not digital, the key controllers and monitors are likely to be digital. Though perhaps only 10 percent of the system is digital, it would only take .001 percent, strategically placed and subject to the date error, to wreak havoc. We can lose robustness if, for example, the alternative source of oil supply or power or critical raw material is no longer available, or if the buffers in the airways and landing sequences that make air traffic so safe disappear because transponders cannot be read, an approaching storm is undetected, and the radio channels are clogged or not working.
Problems with air transport are legion. Air Traffic Control (ATC) is built in part around forty huge mainframe computers that IBM stopped shipping ten years ago. According to IBM, the skills and tools do not exist to even conduct an assessment; replacing the computers is the recommended solution but the FAA does not have the budget to do so now. Here is an example of the many problems and potentials: the FAA team found a monthly command that allows the computer to switch from one cooling pump to another; date-sensitive, the command would not be activated, and the computers would overheat and fail. According to Matthew L. Wald's report, "experts say there could be many such land mines—buried in millions of lines of computer code—that could cause failures for days, weeks, or months after the new year" (Wald 1998).
The problem is not that so many things will fail (though this is possible), but that it just might be critical things which fail, even if there are only a few. (The alternative is also possible: the failures fortunately may not occur in critical applications.) Furthermore, the failure of these mission critical things may be due to a sequence of quite prosaic failures, a sequence that is unimagined because it was inconceivable that things would be failing at the same moment. We may well handle, with great inconvenience and expense, the mounting failures in December, and the declining ones in February, but the chips of January 1 to 3 will all be laid down at once.
Pessimists predict that economic depression will spread rapidly after the due date. It is easy to see. As noted, even the manufacturing plant moves to the complexly interactive/tightly coupled quadrant of NAT with Y2K. According to Internet commentator Ed Yardeni (1988):
When asked about Y2K, Ralph J. Szgenda, the chief information officer of General Motors, told Fortune (April 27, 1998) that there are "catastrophic problems" in every GM plant. I called the reporter to verify this shockingly blunt quote and was informed that the word "catastrophic" was repeated several times during the interview with GM's top IT [Information Technology] man.
In 1997, when Chrysler Corp. turned all the clocks to December 31, 1999, at its Sterling Heights Assembly Plant, the security system shut down and wouldn't let anybody out [from Detroit Free Press, April 23,1998].
In a turn worthy of a Pynchon novel, a Florence, Arizona, prison was reported to have made the same tests, but in this case the security system opened all doors! Other scenarios include goods that cannot be produced or, if produced, delivered or, if delivered, paid for, that will pile up or not appear; payrolls that cannot be met will result in people being laid off; loans that cannot be had will leave debts unpaid; and, in the extreme case, not enough money would circulate. Markets are sensitive and highly coupled now that we have global twenty-four-hour trading, global product interdependency, and just-in-time suppliers. In a rare burst of pessimism from a government official, the Commissioner of the IRS told the Wall Street Journal about Y2K:
There's no point in sugarcoating the problem. If we don't fix the century-date problem, we will have a situation scarier than the average disaster movie you might see on a Sunday night. Twenty-one months from now, there could be 90 million taxpayers who won't get their refunds, and 95% of the revenue stream of the United States could be jeopardized. (April 22,1998)
But note the date: April 1998. The IRS reportedly has caught up since then, and everything will supposedly be fine
As bad as a widespread economic depression will be, it will only produce a vast slowdown and attendant political instability. But what if the production of electric power were to fail? Then, except for vehicles and those emergency and other devices that run on gas, oil, or propane (whose supply in a tank is very limited), it all goes down. In fact, so will the pumps to replenish the tank and many ignition devices for oil and propane. The northern states would quickly freeze and this would cause more devastation than the Canadian ice storm of 1998 because there would be no untouched areas to supply emergency crews and supplies—the interconnectivity again. Since a failure of electricity is the most fearsome possibility, let's take a closer look at what the optimists and pessimists say. It will be our last example, but it is very representative.
Electric Power
The electric industry is unique among industries and systems in three ways. It is the lifeblood of our modern society; without it, most things we depend upon would fail. The second unique aspect of power systems is that electricity is the original and ultimate example of the "just-in-time" system we have introduced into manufacturing, increasing its tight coupling. Electricity cannot be stockpiled in large quantities to tide us over until we get the system fixed. A third unique feature is that the electric systems in North America are tightly interconnected within and between four major electrical interconnections known as "grids," and balancing the flow within these grids is a complicated and delicate operation. The president of the North American Electric Reliability Council, Michael Gent, described the North American power grid as "a very complex system. It's probably the most complex system ever invented by man, more complicated than a moon shot." (Though there are occasional disruptions, grid management has been quite reliable. It has not been tested with multiple, widespread disruptions, however.)
The first detailed report is the September 17, 1998, status report by the North American Electric Reliability Council (NERC), prepared for the U.S. Department of Energy (Council 1998). As three Web critics point out, almost in unison, its optimistic summary belies the paucity of reliable data and the recognition of serious problems buried in the eighty-eight-page report (Cowles 1998b; Garris 1998; Mills 1998). The report is based on 200 "bulk power entities" (regional power pools and Independent System Operators), who in turn drew upon information apparently requested from some 3,200 utilities. The entities summarized the data from the utilities and submitted it to the NERC, an occasion for substantial slippage since there is no verification and considerable incentive to fudge. Indeed, the incentive to not report is strong because of liability potentials, one of the biggest issues in Y2K.
The Council's report is quite detailed on the Y2K "bug," and shows that it is more complex than mistaking the year 2000 for the year 1900. "Data related anomalies may occur at 1/1/99, 9/9/99, 2/29/00 and up to a dozen other dates. August 22, 1999, for example, has been identified as a date when clocks may expire in the Global Positioning Satellites used to provide time signals to some electric power controls centers." The top priority date is the rollover to 2000. The second priority dates are rollover into and out of the leap year date (February 28 to March 1,2004), and September 8, 1999 to September 9, 1999, because of the special value of the date 090999. Third priority dates are the rollover from August 21 to August 22, 1999, when the global positioning system satellite clocks expire, and April 8 to April 9, 1999, due to the special value of the ninety-ninth day of 1999. At least all the problems do not come on one date, and we will have warnings for some time in 1999 of some of the problems.
The report understands the complexity of embedded chip problem. "Electronic chips are generally mass-produced without knowing the ultimate application of the chip. A single circuit board can have 20 to 50 of these chips from various manufacturers. Because of the diversity of chip suppliers, one vendor may use a different mix of chips even within devices labeled with the same name, the number, and year." "It is estimated that less than one to two percent of these devices may use the time/date function in a manner that could result in a Y2K malfunction of the device." This is the going estimate in the Y2K field, but one percent of a huge number is a lot, and it depends upon their connection to, or presence in, critical operations.
The report does say "it is likely that not all Y2K deficiencies will be identified, fixed, and tested in the remaining time." There will be "workarounds," manual overrides, and temporary fixes. For this reason it does not speak of Y2K compliance, but Y2K readiness, meaning that the utilities are only "suitable for continued use into the year 2000"; possibly, it would seem, under degraded conditions. Remediation, thus, seems to mean an ability to cope with disturbances, not necessarily to prevent them. For a Normal Accident theorist, in systems of moderate interactive complexity and tight coupling within themselves, and tight coupling to other vulnerable systems of supplies and distributions, coping is expected to be problematical.
The optimism of the report is indicated by these quotes from the summary: "at this point, the perceived operating risks are manageable. Recent reports in the news media and on the Internet regarding anticipated widespread electrical outages are unsubstantiated. In an industry that meets record peak demands during heat waves and quickly restores service to billions of customers who lose power due to a hurricane or earthquake, preparing for and dealing with operating risk is an ingrained part of the business." Their initial findings indicate that "the impact of Y2K on electrical systems appeared to be less than first anticipated." The anticipated impact must have been seen as very small initially since the industry appears to have been very slow to take up the issue. At the third annual meeting of the only industry-wide meeting addressing the Y2K problem, in March of 1998, only 70 of some 8,000 companies were represented; at a Y2K panel during the annual American Power Conference in 1998 there were only nine people in the audience, four of whom were panel members (Cowles 1998c). According to web commentator Dick Mills, the premier technical conference of the industry in January 1998 had no sessions or committee meetings scheduled for Y2K. When he got on the agenda of one meeting his presentation was blocked "by a bunch of angry people who thought Y2K was a hoax, and that I was a profiteering consultant. A Y2K session for this summer's power meeting in July was canceled because of lack of interest" (emphasis supplied; Mills 1998).
The report's summary is a case of seeing a glass as one-quarter full and neglecting the three-quarters that are empty; its figures are consistently given a positive interpretation. For example, it notes only once that only 75 percent of the electrical suppliers in North America completed and returned the brief nine-page questionnaire from their major trade association. Yet the report claims "it is apparent from this initial round of progress assessment that the industry is taking Y2K very seriously." They should have noted that fully one-quarter apparently did not, though fear of liability may account for some failure to respond, and they may be small producers. (The state of Minnesota had a similar problem with a survey of power companies doing business with the state. In April 1998, of 177 power providers queried, 73 did not respond; of the responders, over 50 percent had no Y2K program in effect.) Only 64 percent of the bulk power entities under the NERC umbrella have a written Y2K plan. These are key distribution companies, for whom a written plan would seem to be essential for making any credible assessment and remediation and testing plan. Cowles wonders how the remaining 36 percent of the responding companies could have given reliable responses without a written plan. Most of the responding companies are still in the assessment stage or the awareness stage. The remediation/testing stage is the longest, consuming from 62 to 70 percent of total effort but, of the minority there, most are only 30 percent or less complete. These figures are from a skimpy, unverified, and possibly unrepresentative data set. The optimistic conclusions drawn from it seem unwarranted.
A January 11, 1999, up-date from NERC is even more optimistic, claiming 98 percent of the facilities reported; remediation/testing for billing problems comes out on top at 58 percent of facilities; but nuclear power stations, which might be expected to have a higher priority are only at 31 percent (Ratcliffe 1999). It could be that they are harder to fix, but since they do not expect any problems with nuclear facilities it must just reflect a lower priority. Rick Cowles analyzed the data the NERC used for its report and wrote a report before they did. Rather than 98 percent participation of the 254 electric industry "reporting entities," it turns out to still be about 75 percent! Only 58 percent of survey respondents—that is, not including the 25 percent not reporting—had started looking at contingency planning for Y2K. (A smaller group, the Independent Power Producers, which are non-utility generators, account for 12 percent of net generating capacity, but only ten of them, mostly the smaller ones, reported to the survey in November.) The goal of being Y2K ready by May 31, 1999, will not be met by 71 percent of the "reporting entities," and so on (Cowles 1999). Nevertheless, the press stories remained optimistic. For example, a CNN web report for February 24, 1999, quotes Janet Benini of the U.S. Transportation Department as saying, "The department is confident that electric power will not be a Y2K problem."
Electric companies are far from stand-alone, self-contained islands of production, and they have three major dependencies that may cause problems—our interconnectivity problem: 1) They cannot generate or deliver electricity without telecommunications, and telecommunications cannot operate without electricity, a classic Catch 22 situation. Very close coordination will be required between these two industries, but there is no evidence of a major effort in this direction. The report is not comforting when it notes "the challenge is that some operating entities may be dependent on 50 or more external communications service providers." 2) The second dependency is on an available fuel supply and its delivery. This also requires close coordination, in this case between the electric power industry and mining, refining, trucking, rail, pipelines, and so on. This dependency is noted but not assessed in the report, and perhaps it is not threatening. Almost all we know about this sector is that a Senate committee poll of transportation companies says that trucking and the railroads are closer to compliance than are airports—at least 80 percent responded to the poll (Clausing 1998). These two considerations might mean that even if the plant itself is compliant, and running on year 2000 (de Jaeger says this is true of dozens of plants), telecommunication and supplies might do them in. 3) Finally, as the report does point out, Independent Power Producers have no service obligations to be able to provide base load power for regional bulk power entities. Yet they provide a significant contribution to the overall energy mix in the U.S., particularly on the East and West coasts. They can have a major impact on regional grid stability issues, yet there is little in the way of Y2K status reports from this industry sector. As Cowles concludes, the report constitutes an unaudited performance monitoring of the key industry in industrial society, and it is by the industry itself.
We might add that the Council declares that the government has no business monitoring the industry with respect to Y2K. But the industry is in turmoil. It is, the report notes "in the middle of a major restructuring to introduce wholesale and retail competition for electricity. Attention has been on competing in the marketplace, cutting costs, mergers, reorganizations, and survival. The reality is that industry restructuring is moving rapidly and cannot be temporarily halted to address Y2K" (emphasis supplied). Merge; don't fix. The mergers, the Council admits, are limiting the information sharing that it admits "remains alarmingly low for an industry that is used to open cooperation on technical and reliability issues." Even so, a concern with Y2K should not slow the merger process, they optimistically insist. Furthermore, they assert that the government should keep its hands off. "Allow the industry to continue managing Y2K efforts. Government intervention in the form of additional reporting requirements or deadlines will dilute already strained resources. Feedback on overall goals and effectiveness of Y2K efforts should be provided through the existing industry led program." Presumably, the 25 percent of bulk providers that did not respond to the questionnaire should be left alone. (Of course, the government has one role—the Council says it should protect the industry from litigation arising from the information sharing process, and it has.)
The view from the trenches is quite different. Cowles gives an example of just the boiler control of a U.K. Fossil Station that was reviewed for Y2K impact. It took five people three months to complete the analysis on this single system in the plant, and that did not include repairs. Scaled to the entire plant, and this is only a fossil fuel power station, you can see what the industry is up against. Cowles is close to hysterical in another posting on the e-mail; but the Electrical Power Research Institute, the major research and support systems of the industry, sounds quite optimistic in their web page. Fully 70 percent of the generating capacity in the U.S. has joined in their effort, they say, and everyone is working hard. The testimony of their spokesperson before a Senate special committee in June of 1998 was quite unspecific about the particulars of the effort and any indications of success. Their program did not even start until the fall of 1997.
Here is some material from another sceptic, Roleigh Martin, presented in the Y2K Today web site. Martin quotes an anonymous source, who attended a state session on Y2K and embedded systems in electric utilities in a Midwestern state in 1997:
In the testing of two coal fire power plants (which were currently offline and being used as "hot spares") for year 2000 compliance, the clocks were simultaneously rolled over to the year 2000, causing immediate plant failure. In an attempt to better understand the failure, the roll over test was repeated. In the second test, the plants again failed, but a different embedded controller was determined to be at fault. The roll over test was repeated a third time in hopes of replicating one of the previous failures. In this test, the plants failed from yet a different embedded controller. It was determined that this last failure would have caused a grid wide failure had the plants been online. It took 13 days in order to restore the plants to working condition from the last failure. (1998)
Unfortunately, this is hearsay, and should be treated as such, but in my experience with complex systems it seems plausible. We do not have a similar insider's account from a nuclear utility, where boiling water is considerably more complicated. Here is what the Council says about these scary things: "Y2K issues in nuclear facilities do not represent the public health or safety issue. No nuclear generating plant has found the Y2K problem in safety systems that would have prevented safe plant shutdown at the tum-of-the-century." This finding confirms a September 1997 letter and the Nuclear Regulatory Commission staff policy paper that concluded, " … safety related initiation and actuation systems (e.g., reactor trip systems, engineered safety feature actuation systems) are not subject to the year 2000 concern." All nuclear plants are expected to be Y2K ready by March 31, 1999. "Relatively few digital components have been identified as having year 2000 deficiencies. Those found were quickly remedied. At each facility there are a few components that are challenging to test or require extensive and costly remediation programs. Thus, a small percentage of the items drive most of the effort." Since these plants have a hard time trying to avoid unplanned shutdowns under normal conditions, the addition of "a small percentage of items" that are recalcitrant and, as far as I know, show no evidence of having engaged in on-line testing (which may be impossible), is not grounds for encouragement. Nor is this report from the Cassandra Project, based on NRC documents: "Also recently, the NRC discovered that an order of 600 high-end computers failed to pass Y2K tests. It also discovered that new 200 MHz Pentium PCs bought in January (1997) have a problem with an internal clock on the PCs' motherboards. Dallas Semiconductor readily admits that the realtime clocks used in the PCs are not compliant" (1997). A news story from Rockville, Maryland, details how a Peach Bottom nuclear plant near York, Pennsylvania, recently experienced a seven-hour lockup of the plant's primary and backup plant monitoring system computers during Y2K testing. The NRC weekly summary of February 12, 1999, reports that operators lost the plant's Safety Parameter Display System (SPDS), Emergency Response Data System (ERDS), and 3D Monicore thermal limit monitoring system during the event (The Newsroom 1999).
This accident makes Rick Cowles's possible scenario more believable:
Here's an example. In the days following 01/01/2000, let's assume that a plant has some type of transient that causes an automatic shutdown (a relatively routine event). What would happen should the event recorder (computer) completely and unrecoverably crash during a routine SCRAM or plant trip? If you've ever had the bad fortune to be in the control room during a garden variety SCRAM, you know that automatic system responses are happening much too quickly to analyze total plant status while attempting to control and stabilize the plant. Event logging is the only way to understand the big picture (while the event is in progress), and reconstruct the event (after it's over). If you don't have event logging, you can't understand what's happening in your plant. Even making the rash assumption that everything else worked O.K. and Y2K didn't raise its ugly head in some embedded logic somewhere…. if event logging is inoperable, the plant is in an UNANALYZED CONDITION.
Cowles continues:
There is a growing concern in all sectors of the industry that every nuclear power facility in the U.S. which has not conclusively proven Y2K compliance may be required to shut down prior to the end of 1999. The NRC has publicly stated that they will require certification of Year 2000 readiness from every nuclear plant in the country. In the absence of that certification, the NRC has no recourse but to require the shutdown, prior to 01/01/2000, of the plants that haven't provided this certification. (1998a)
Cowles exaggerates the determination of the NRC, and the issue is complex, but required shut-downs could occur.
All grids use nuclear power; it constitutes about a quarter of our electrical energy. Many such shutdowns would be hard to accommodate, even if every nonnuclear utility functioned flawlessly. Living in the northeast (40 percent dependent on nuclear power), my best prediction can be found in my plan to buy a gasoline generator, but not to hoard cash or food.
Y2K is that rare potential disaster that we can see coming, can plan for, and can prognosticate about. Predictions follow the expected pattern. Those at the helm are optimistic, social commentators are pessimistic, and most social scientists duck their heads and fail to exercise the predictive skills their learning should call for. Properly viewed, this is an opportunity to test theories about organizational mind sets and organizational interests in all three cases. It gives us the chance to line up the players and the predictions and, more important in the case of social scientists, to test our theories of crisis management (from denial through preparedness to coping). It pits the importance of the newly enlarged global economy and the "mechanical" and unforgiving coupling of society that runs on cheap oil and electronics against the "organic" coupling of a dense web of resilient devices and human relationships. This is an event we should profit from, even though we dread it. Its potential scale and scope dwarfs all other "normal accidents" discussed in the book. But the tools discussed in Normal Accidents would appear to be among the most relevant available.

Since a new ship built in the U.S. will cost almost three times as much as one built in Japan, we continue to use dreadfully unsafe World War II ships and have far and away the oldest fleet in the world.
